lessonTitle: Humid Air Properties: Humidity Ratio, Relative Humidity, Dew Point and Enthalpy

blocks.text: On a humid afternoon the windows of a cold-drinks warehouse fog up the moment a loading door opens, even though the outside air is warm. The cold glass is below the dew point of the incoming air, so water condenses on it. Predicting that, and the energy needed to cool and dry the air, starts with a handful of properties of moist air: humidity ratio, relative humidity, dew point and enthalpy.

blocks.markdown: Atmospheric air is a mixture of dry air and water vapour, and both behave as ideal gases at the conditions of interest. By **Dalton's law**, the total pressure is $P = P_a + P_v$, where $P_a$ is the partial pressure of dry air and $P_v$ the partial pressure of water vapour. The amount of water vapour is described by the **humidity ratio** (also called specific humidity) $\omega$, the mass of vapour per kg of dry air.

blocks.title: Humidity ratio, relative humidity, dew point
blocks.text: Humidity ratio $\omega = m_v/m_a$ (kg vapour per kg dry air). Relative humidity $\varphi = P_v/P_g$, the ratio of the vapour partial pressure to the saturation pressure $P_g$ at the same dry-bulb temperature. Dew-point temperature $T_{dp}$ is the temperature at which vapour begins to condense when air is cooled at constant pressure and constant $\omega$; it equals $T_{sat}$ at $P_v$.

blocks.caption: The factor 0.622 is $M_v/M_a = 18.02/28.97$. $P$ in kPa (101.325 kPa at sea level); $P_g$ from steam tables at the dry-bulb temperature.
Saturation pressure of water (typical steam-table values, rounded).

blocks.title: Humidity ratio, dew point and enthalpy
blocks.prompt: Air at $T = 25$ °C, $P = 101.325$ kPa has a relative humidity of 60%. Use $P_g(25\ °C) = 3.169$ kPa. Find the vapour pressure, humidity ratio, dew point and specific enthalpy.

steps.text: Vapour pressure from the definition of $\varphi$.
Dew point: the temperature with $P_g = 1.901$ kPa. Between 16 °C (1.818 kPa) and 17 °C (1.938 kPa), by interpolation.
Enthalpy per kg of dry air, with $T$ in °C: sensible part of dry air plus enthalpy of the vapour.

blocks.answer: P_v = 1.901 kPa, ω = 0.0119, dew point ≈ 16.7 °C, h ≈ 55.4 kJ/kg dry air.

blocks.caption: $T$ in °C, $c_{p,a} = 1.005$ kJ/(kg K); 2501 kJ/kg is the enthalpy of saturated vapour at 0 °C and 1.82 kJ/(kg K) the specific heat of vapour. Enthalpy is per kg of **dry air**.

blocks.markdown: A **psychrometric chart** plots $\omega$ against dry-bulb temperature at one pressure. Curves of constant relative humidity rise to the right (concave upward, since $\omega$ at fixed $\varphi$ increases with temperature), with the saturation curve ($\varphi = 100\%$) as the upper boundary. Constant-$h$ lines slope down to the right, almost parallel to the constant wet-bulb lines, and are read from a scale on the diagonal. Any two independent properties (for example $T$ and $\varphi$, or $T$ and $\omega$) fix the state at a given total pressure, and the chart gives the rest. The chart is an accurate display of the equations above, so a chart reading can be checked by calculation.

blocks.title: State from dry-bulb temperature and humidity ratio
blocks.prompt: Air at $T = 30$ °C and $P = 101.325$ kPa has $\omega = 0.0112$. Find $\varphi$, the dew point and the enthalpy. Use $P_g(30\ °C) = 4.246$ kPa.

steps.text: Dew point: $P_g = 1.792$ kPa lies between 15 °C (1.706) and 16 °C (1.818).

blocks.answer: φ ≈ 42%, dew point ≈ 15.8 °C, h ≈ 58.8 kJ/kg dry air.

blocks.title: Heating and cooling at constant $\omega$
blocks.text: Sensible heating or cooling changes $T$ and $\varphi$ but not $\omega$ or the dew point. Heating air lowers its relative humidity; cooling it raises it until it reaches 100% at the dew point, after which water condenses and $\omega$ falls.

items: $\omega$ is per kg of dry air; masses of moist air include the vapour: $m = m_a(1+\omega)$.
At fixed $P_v$, a lower total pressure (altitude) gives a larger $\omega$.
Relative humidity depends on dry-bulb temperature; humidity ratio and dew point do not change with sensible heat.
Wet-bulb temperature lies between the dew point and dry-bulb temperature, and equals both at saturation.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Do not use $P_v$ in place of $P - P_v$ in the denominator. Use $P_g$ at the dry-bulb temperature, not at the dew point, for $\varphi$. Keep $h$ per kg of dry air; do not divide by $1+\omega$ unless a per-kg-of-mixture value is requested.

points: Dew point is the saturation temperature at the partial pressure of the vapour.
The psychrometric chart displays these relations; two properties fix the state at a given pressure.

questions.stem: The humidity ratio of moist air at total pressure $P$ and vapour partial pressure $P_v$ is

distractorRationale.a: The denominator must be the partial pressure of dry air, $P - P_v$.
distractorRationale.d: Uses the inverse ratio of molar masses.

questions.explanation: The ratio of the masses is $m_v/m_a = (M_v/M_a)(P_v/P_a)$ with $P_a = P - P_v$. With $M_v/M_a = 0.622$ this gives the standard expression.

questions.stem: The dew-point temperature of moist air is best defined as

options.text: the temperature at which condensation begins when the air is cooled at constant pressure and humidity ratio
the temperature at which the relative humidity is 50%
the dry-bulb temperature at which $\omega$ is zero
the temperature reading of a wetted thermometer

questions.correctOptionText: the temperature at which condensation begins when the air is cooled at constant pressure and humidity ratio

distractorRationale.b: Dew point corresponds to 100% relative humidity.
distractorRationale.c: $\omega$ is not zero for humid air.

questions.explanation: On cooling at constant $\omega$ and $P$, $P_v$ is unchanged while $P_g$ falls until $P_g = P_v$. This is the dew point, equal to $T_{sat}(P_v)$.

questions.stem: Moist air is heated in a duct at constant pressure with no moisture added. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The humidity ratio increases and the relative humidity decreases
The dew point rises and the relative humidity is unchanged
The humidity ratio and the relative humidity are both unchanged
The humidity ratio and dew point are unchanged and the relative humidity decreases

questions.correctOptionText: The humidity ratio and dew point are unchanged and the relative humidity decreases

distractorRationale.a: No moisture is added, so $\omega$ is constant.
distractorRationale.b: The dew point depends only on $P_v$, which is constant.
distractorRationale.c: The saturation pressure rises with $T$, so $\varphi = P_v/P_g$ falls.

questions.explanation: Sensible heating changes only the dry-bulb temperature. Since $P_v$ is fixed and $P_g$ rises with $T$, $\varphi$ falls, while $\omega$ and the dew point are unaffected.

questions.stem: Air at 28 °C with a humidity ratio of 0.0100 kg/kg dry air is read on a psychrometric chart. Which enthalpy (kJ/kg dry air) does the equation $h = 1.005T + \omega(2501 + 1.82T)$ give?

distractorRationale.a: This is only the dry-air term, neglecting the vapour enthalpy.
distractorRationale.c: This is only the vapour term, neglecting the dry air.
distractorRationale.d: Omits the $1.82\,T$ term in the vapour enthalpy.

questions.explanation: Dry-air term: $1.005\times28 = 28.14$ kJ/kg. Vapour term: $0.0100\times(2501 + 1.82\times28) = 25.52$ kJ/kg. The sum is 53.66 kJ/kg dry air, which is what the enthalpy scale would give.

questions.stem: Two air samples have the same vapour partial pressure but one is at a lower total pressure (a high-altitude site). How do their humidity ratios compare?

options.text: The sample at lower total pressure has the smaller humidity ratio
They are equal because $P_v$ is the same
The sample at lower total pressure has the larger humidity ratio
The humidity ratio is independent of pressure

questions.correctOptionText: The sample at lower total pressure has the larger humidity ratio

distractorRationale.a: $P - P_v$ is smaller, so $\omega$ is larger.
distractorRationale.b: The total pressure appears in the denominator.

questions.explanation: In $\omega = 0.622P_v/(P - P_v)$, lowering $P$ shrinks the denominator and raises $\omega$ for the same $P_v$. The same mass of dry air occupies more volume at altitude, so there is more vapour per kg of dry air.

questions.stem: Moist air at 101.325 kPa has a water-vapour partial pressure of 1.20 kPa. Calculate the humidity ratio in kg of vapour per kg of dry air.
questions.explanation: $\omega = 0.622\times1.20/(101.325 - 1.20) = 0.7464/100.125 = 0.00745$. This is about 7.5 g of water per kg of dry air.

questions.stem: Air at 30 °C has a vapour partial pressure of 2.00 kPa. The saturation pressure of water at 30 °C is 4.246 kPa. Calculate the relative humidity in %.
At a mountain site the total pressure is 90 kPa. Air at 30 °C has a humidity ratio of 0.0140 kg/kg dry air. Using $P_g(30\ °C) = 4.246$ kPa, calculate the relative humidity in %.
questions.explanation: Invert the humidity-ratio equation: $P_v = \omega P/(0.622 + \omega) = 0.0140\times90/0.636 = 1.981$ kPa. Then $\varphi = 1.981/4.246 = 0.4666$, or 46.7%.

questions.stem: A polished metal plate is cooled slowly in a room where the air is at 24 °C. Mist first appears on the plate when its surface temperature reaches 12 °C. Explain this using the dew point, and determine the relative humidity of the room air.
markingGuide: Air next to the glass is cooled at nearly constant pressure and humidity ratio
When its temperature falls to the dew point, $P_v = P_g(T)$ and relative humidity reaches 100%
Below the dew point, vapour condenses on the glass
The dew point of the room air is therefore the temperature at which the glass just mists, here 12 °C
$P_v = P_g(12\ °C) \approx 1.40$ kPa and the relative humidity is $P_v/P_g(24\ °C) \approx 1.40/2.98 \approx 0.47$ (about 47%)
Notes the dew point depends only on $P_v$ (the moisture content), not on the dry-bulb temperature
questions.explanation: Condensation starts when the glass temperature equals the dew point of the room air. At the dew point $P_v = P_g(12\ °C)$, which gives a room relative humidity of about 47% at 24 °C (typical saturation pressures: 1.40 kPa at 12 °C, 2.98 kPa at 24 °C).

questions.stem: Air at 30 °C, 101.325 kPa and 50% relative humidity (take $P_g = 4.246$ kPa) flows through a duct. (a) Calculate its humidity ratio. (b) Calculate its enthalpy per kg of dry air and the sensible and latent shares. (c) Explain how you would read the same enthalpy from a psychrometric chart.
markingGuide: Chart: locate the state at 30 °C dry-bulb and the 50% curve, read $\omega$ on the right-hand axis, and follow the constant-enthalpy line up-left to the enthalpy scale on the saturation curve boundary
States that enthalpy is quoted per kg of dry air and that the chart is drawn for one total pressure
questions.explanation: The humidity ratio is 0.01331, giving $h = 64.2$ kJ/kg dry air, of which 30.1 kJ/kg is the dry-air term and 34.0 kJ/kg the vapour term. On the chart the state is the intersection of the 30 °C line with the 50% curve, and the enthalpy is read along the sloping line to the scale.
